# Dollar RMSE for one set of predictions.
rmse <- function(obs, pred) {
  sqrt(mean((obs - pred)^2))
}

# Round a number of dollars for the prose.
dollars <- function(x) {
  out <- rep("—", length(x))
  ok <- !is.na(x)
  out[ok] <- paste0(
    ifelse(x[ok] < 0, "-", ""),
    "$",
    formatC(round(abs(x[ok])), format = "f", big.mark = ",", digits = 0)
  )
  out
}

pct <- function(x) {
  paste0(formatC(round(100 * x, 1), format = "f", digits = 1), "%")
}

times_word <- function(x) {
  formatC(round(x, 1), format = "f", digits = 1)
}

range_words <- function(lo, hi) paste(dollars(lo), "to", dollars(hi))

show_p <- function(p) {
  ifelse(
    is.na(p),
    "—",
    ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", paste0("= ", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3)))
  )
}

# Linear combination of coefficients, with a t interval.
# weights is a named vector on the coefficient scale.
contrast <- function(model, weights) {
  b <- coef(model)
  L <- setNames(rep(0, length(b)), names(b))
  unknown <- setdiff(names(weights), names(b))
  if (length(unknown)) stop("Not in the model: ", paste(unknown, collapse = ", "))
  L[names(weights)] <- weights
  est <- sum(L * b)
  se <- sqrt(drop(t(L) %*% vcov(model) %*% L))
  df <- df.residual(model)
  tcrit <- qt(0.975, df)
  tstat <- est / se
  data.frame(
    estimate = est,
    std_error = se,
    lcl = est - tcrit * se,
    ucl = est + tcrit * se,
    t = tstat,
    p_value = 2 * pt(-abs(tstat), df)
  )
}

partial_f <- function(reduced, full, comparison) {
  a <- anova(reduced, full)
  data.frame(
    comparison = comparison,
    df = a$Df[2],
    F = a$F[2],
    p_value = a$`Pr(>F)`[2],
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

# AIC, BIC, adjusted R-squared, and PRESS for one lm fit.
# PRESS sums squared leave-one-out errors. It is not a dollar miss.
linear_scores <- function(fit) {
  data.frame(
    AIC = AIC(fit),
    BIC = BIC(fit),
    adj_r2 = summary(fit)$adj.r.squared,
    PRESS = sum((residuals(fit) / (1 - hatvalues(fit)))^2)
  )
}

resid_summary <- function(model, scale) {
  r <- resid(model)
  s <- model$model$smoker
  data.frame(
    scale = scale,
    sd_nonsmoker = sd(r[s == "no"]),
    sd_smoker = sd(r[s == "yes"]),
    sd_ratio = sd(r[s == "yes"]) / sd(r[s == "no"]),
    skewness = mean((r - mean(r))^3) / sd(r)^3,
    n_rstudent_gt_3 = sum(abs(rstudent(model)) > 3),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

sigma_ci <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)
  s2 <- var(x)
  lower <- sqrt((n - 1) * s2 / qchisq(0.05 / 2, n - 1, lower.tail = FALSE))
  upper <- sqrt((n - 1) * s2 / qchisq(0.05 / 2, n - 1, lower.tail = TRUE))
  c(lower, upper)
}

This notebook is a supplement to Health Care Charges executive brief. The outcome of our analysis may be used to explain a customer bill and predict future health care charges.

Technical analysis is provided in EDA notebooks as well as Objectives 1 & 2 notebooks located in https://github.com/PowellOnPoint/msds-6372-project1-insurance. The code that produces every figure is in this file, folded by default, and repeated in the appendix.

# The equation we would explain. Sex is not in it.
# Smoker reference is no. Region reference is northeast.
explain_formula <- charges ~ age + children + bmi * smoker + region
explain <- lm(explain_formula, data = ins)

no_children <- lm(charges ~ age + bmi * smoker + region, data = ins)
no_region <- lm(charges ~ age + children + bmi * smoker, data = ins)
with_sex <- lm(charges ~ age + sex + children + bmi * smoker + region, data = ins)
with_smoker_region <- lm(
  charges ~ age + children + bmi * smoker + smoker * region,
  data = ins
)
with_age_smoker <- lm(
  charges ~ age * smoker + children + bmi * smoker + region,
  data = ins
)
with_age_region <- lm(
  charges ~ age * region + children + bmi * smoker,
  data = ins
)
with_bmi_region <- lm(
  charges ~ age + children + bmi * smoker + bmi * region,
  data = ins
)
with_both_twoway <- lm(
  charges ~ age + children + (bmi + smoker) * region + bmi:smoker,
  data = ins
)
with_threeway <- lm(
  charges ~ age + children + bmi * smoker * region,
  data = ins
)
additive <- lm(charges ~ age + children + bmi + smoker + region, data = ins)

tests <- bind_rows(

    with_both_twoway,
    with_threeway,

  ),
  partial_f(additive, explain, "Let the BMI slope differ by smoker")
)

cv_lm <- function(formula) {
  fold_rmse <- numeric(length(fold_index))
  for (i in seq_along(fold_index)) {
    fit_rows <- fold_index[[i]]
    score_rows <- setdiff(1:nrow(ins), fit_rows)
    fit_i <- lm(formula, data = ins[fit_rows, ])
    pred_i <- predict(fit_i, newdata = ins[score_rows, ])
    fold_rmse[i] <- rmse(ins$charges[score_rows], pred_i)
  }
  fold_rmse
}

explain_fit <- lm(explain_formula, data = train)
explain_scores <- linear_scores(explain_fit)

# Left-out misses. One prediction per customer, from a fit that did not
# include that customer. Squared miss is the contribution to mean squared error.
oof_rows <- function(formula, search) {
  pred <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(ins))
  for (i in seq_along(fold_index)) {
    fit_rows <- fold_index[[i]]
    score_rows <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(ins)), fit_rows)
    fit_i <- lm(formula, data = ins[fit_rows, ])
    if (search) {
      fit_i <- step(
        fit_i,
        scope = list(lower = ~1, upper = formula),
        direction = "both",
        trace = 0
      )
    }
    pred[score_rows] <- predict(fit_i, newdata = ins[score_rows, ])
  }
  pred
}

pull_oof <- function(fit) {
  p <- fit$pred
  tune_cols <- intersect(names(fit$bestTune), names(p))
  for (col in tune_cols) {
    p <- p[p[[col]] == fit$bestTune[[1, col]], ]
  }
  p <- p[!duplicated(p$rowIndex), ]
  out <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(ins))
  out[p$rowIndex] <- p$pred
  if (anyNA(out)) stop("A left-out customer has no prediction.")
  out
}

oof_control <- trainControl(
  method = "cv",
  number = 10,
  index = fold_index,
  savePredictions = "final"
)
set.seed(1234)
knn_oof_fit <- train(
  np_formula,
  data = ins,
  method = "knn",
  trControl = oof_control,
  preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
  tuneGrid = expand.grid(k = c(1:10, 20, 30))
)
set.seed(1234)
bag_oof_fit <- train(
  np_formula,
  data = ins,
  method = "treebag",
  trControl = oof_control
)
set.seed(1234)
forest_oof_fit <- train(
  np_formula,
  data = ins,
  method = "rf",
  trControl = oof_control,
  tuneLength = 3
)

oof_pred <- data.frame(
  smoker = ins$smoker,
  actual = ins$charges,
  `Explanation equation` = oof_rows(explain_formula, FALSE),
  `All two-way products` = oof_rows(full_formula, FALSE),
  `Term search` = oof_rows(full_formula, TRUE),
  `Shrunk equation` = out_of_fold,
  `Nearest neighbors` = pull_oof(knn_oof_fit),
  `Averaged trees` = pull_oof(bag_oof_fit),
  `Random forest` = pull_oof(forest_oof_fit),
  check.names = FALSE
)

miss_long <- pivot_longer(
  oof_pred,
  cols = all_of(model_levels),
  names_to = "model",
  values_to = "quoted"
)
miss_long$miss <- miss_long$actual - miss_long$quoted
miss_long$squared_miss <- miss_long$miss^2
miss_long$model <- factor(miss_long$model, levels = model_levels)
miss_long$smoker_label <- ifelse(miss_long$smoker == "yes", "Smoker", "Non-smoker")

margin_table <- miss_long %>%
  group_by(model, smoker_label) %>%
  summarise(
    abs95 = quantile(abs(miss), 0.95),
    q025 = quantile(miss, 0.025),
    q975 = quantile(miss, 0.975),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

abs95_of <- function(model_name, smoker_label) {
  margin_table$abs95[
    margin_table$model == model_name &
      margin_table$smoker_label == smoker_label
  ]
}
q_of <- function(model_name, smoker_label, column) {
  margin_table[[column]][
    margin_table$model == model_name &
      margin_table$smoker_label == smoker_label
  ]
}
forest_abs95_yes <- abs95_of("Random forest", "Smoker")
forest_abs95_no <- abs95_of("Random forest", "Non-smoker")
explain_abs95_yes <- abs95_of("Explanation equation", "Smoker")
explain_abs95_no <- abs95_of("Explanation equation", "Non-smoker")
forest_q025_yes <- q_of("Random forest", "Smoker", "q025")
forest_q975_yes <- q_of("Random forest", "Smoker", "q975")
forest_q025_no <- q_of("Random forest", "Non-smoker", "q025")
forest_q975_no <- q_of("Random forest", "Non-smoker", "q975")
explain_q025_yes <- q_of("Explanation equation", "Smoker", "q025")
explain_q975_yes <- q_of("Explanation equation", "Smoker", "q975")
explain_q025_no <- q_of("Explanation equation", "Non-smoker", "q025")
explain_q975_no <- q_of("Explanation equation", "Non-smoker", "q975")

write.csv(margin_table, "talk_margins.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# The mean absolute miss is pulled by the tail. The median is the
# middle customer: half the bills are closer to the quote than this.
center_by <- miss_long %>%
  group_by(model, smoker_label) %>%
  summarise(
    median_abs = median(abs(miss)),
    mean_abs = mean(abs(miss)),
    rmse = sqrt(mean(squared_miss)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
center_all <- miss_long %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  summarise(
    median_abs = median(abs(miss)),
    mean_abs = mean(abs(miss)),
    rmse = sqrt(mean(squared_miss)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
pick_median <- function(frame, group) {
  rows <- frame[frame$smoker_label == group, ]
  as.character(rows$model[which.min(rows$median_abs)])
}
best_med_yes <- pick_median(center_by, "Smoker")
best_med_no <- pick_median(center_by, "Non-smoker")
best_med <- as.character(center_all$model[which.min(center_all$median_abs)])
med_of <- function(model_name, group) {
  center_by$median_abs[
    center_by$model == model_name & center_by$smoker_label == group
  ]
}
mean_of <- function(model_name, group) {
  center_by$mean_abs[
    center_by$model == model_name & center_by$smoker_label == group
  ]
}
med_f_yes <- med_of("Random forest", "Smoker")
med_f_no <- med_of("Random forest", "Non-smoker")
mean_f_yes <- mean_of("Random forest", "Smoker")
mean_f_no <- mean_of("Random forest", "Non-smoker")
med_e_yes <- med_of("Explanation equation", "Smoker")
med_e_no <- med_of("Explanation equation", "Non-smoker")
mean_e_yes <- mean_of("Explanation equation", "Smoker")
mean_e_no <- mean_of("Explanation equation", "Non-smoker")
med_f <- center_all$median_abs[center_all$model == "Random forest"]
mean_f <- center_all$mean_abs[center_all$model == "Random forest"]
write.csv(center_by, "talk_center.csv", row.names = FALSE)

The Big Picture

Smoking status dominates the bill, followed by BMI, children then age. Smokers are 20.5% of these 1,337 customers, and their average charges are 3.8 times the non-smoker average: $32,050 versus $8,441.

Holding age, number of children, and region fixed, mean charges for a smoker at BMI 30 are $22,833 (279.7%) higher than for a non-smoker at the same BMI. The range we would quote, from one thousand resamples of whole customers, is $22,045 to $23,566. At BMI 25 our best estimate is $15,643, and $30,024 at BMI 35. Among smokers, each extra BMI point is associated with about $1,461 more. Among non-smokers, the BMI slope is not clearly different from zero.

The smoking result does not clearly change by region. Region does shift the level of the bill. After age, children, BMI, and smoking status are held fixed, the southeast average is $1,207 lower than the northeast, and the southwest average is $1,228 lower. The unadjusted southeast average looks high because that region has more smokers and a higher BMI, not because the region itself adds cost once those facts are in the equation.

Each additional year of age is associated with $264 higher mean charges in both groups, about 2.0% of the average bill. Each additional child is associated with $512. Sex is not clearly associated with charges once the other facts are held fixed.

We recommend a random forest prediction model due to the variability in charges. The prediction model is not easy to interpret, refer to the equation to drive conversations.

Margin of errors were constructed by leaving each customer out of the fit once. 95% of errors were within $9,800 for smokers and $12,486 for non-smokers. The explanation equation’s margins on the same customers are $9,489 for smokers and $13,031 for non-smokers. We compared this cross-validation to a 20% validation test to illustrate a bias-variance trade-off between models.

These averages are still dominated by a few customers in the sample. For example, half of smoker bills fell within $1,111 of the prediction model’s quote, against an average absolute error of $2,198. Half of non-smoker bills fell within $1,428, against an average of $2,718. Using the median, the closest smoker quote is the random forest, and the closest non-smoker quote is the nearest neighbors by only $26. We still recommend a random forest method for prediction after considering both average and median.

The forest is $2,925 closer than the equation for the typical smoker. Use the forest to score because, once BMI is high, its quote levels off with the smoker cloud instead of climbing past it in a straight line, and because the typical customer is closer to that quote than the average error suggests. Use the equation when someone asks why the bill moved.

Data Summary

We used 1,337 distinct customers in four US regions in our sample. They are not a random sample of the country. Smoking was not assigned. The intervals describe this file. They are not a causal effect of smoking, weight, or region, and they are not a guarantee for one future person.

The file arrived with 1,338 rows and 0 missing cells. One exact duplicate was a 19-year-old northwest man, a non-smoker, BMI 30.59, no children, charges $1,639.56. The extra copy is dropped in this code. The file on disk is not edited. Every number below uses 1,337 customers. Charges run from $1,122 to $63,770.

Skewness

The average bill is $13,279 and the median is $9,386, illustrating a right-skewed distribution. We consider large bills to be a representative sample and retain them when modeling to influence performance.

Among smokers the correlation is 0.81. Among non-smokers it is 0.08. One smoking coefficient, with a single BMI slope, would average a steep line and a flat line into a number that is true for neither group. The Equation

\[ \text{charges} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{age} + \beta_2 \text{children} + \beta_3 \text{bmi} + \beta_4 \text{smoker} + \beta_5 (\text{bmi} \times \text{smoker}) + \text{region} + \varepsilon \]

Smoking reference is non-smoker. Region reference is northeast. Sex is not in the equation. The smoker coefficient by itself is the gap at BMI 0, which is not practical. We quote at BMI 25, 30, and 35.

Each row in the table below is a nested comparison against the equation above, or against the equation with the extra terms the row needs. A small p-value means the extra term improves the fit enough that chance is a poor explanation. It is not, by itself, a reason to add complexity.

test_show <- tests
test_show$F <- round(test_show$F, 2)
test_show$p_value <- show_p(test_show$p_value)
names(test_show) <- c("Comparison", "Extra df", "F", "p-value")
test_show
Comparison Extra df F p-value
Add children 1 21.54 < 0.001
Add sex 1 3.50 = 0.062
Add region as a level shift 3 4.61 = 0.003
Let the smoker gap differ by region 3 1.20 = 0.308
Let the age slope differ by smoker 1 0.01 = 0.918
Let the age slope differ by region 3 1.28 = 0.279
Let the BMI slope differ by region 3 3.76 = 0.011
Let the smoker BMI slope differ by region 3 1.56 = 0.197
Let the BMI slope differ by smoker 1 746.10 < 0.001

Children stay. Sex stays out (p = 0.062). Region stays as a level shift. Letting the smoker gap differ by region does not clearly improve the fit (p = 0.308). Letting the age slope differ by smoking status does not clearly improve the dollar equation (p = 0.918). Letting the age slope differ by region does not either.

Letting the BMI slope differ by region marginally improves the fit (p = 0.011), but is confounded by demographics already included in the equation. The non-smoker BMI slope is small and does not provide enough evidence to support adding complexity. The southeast difference on that small slope is reported as a test, not as four new columns in the main table. Once both region products are available, letting the smoker BMI slope differ by region does not provide enough evidence to justify complexity (p = 0.197).

The product of BMI and smoking status is not optional. Dropping it, after age, children, and region are already in the equation, provide overwhelm evidence of a difference in predictive power (p < 0.001).

Insights

Holding BMI, smoking status, number of children, and region fixed, each additional year of age is associated with $264 higher mean charges. The ordinary 95% range is $245 to $283. The paired resampling range, which keeps each customer with their own residual error, is $245 to $283. The same year-of-age amount fits smokers and non-smokers at about 2.0% of the average bill.

Holding age, number of children, and region fixed, the difference in mean charges between a smoker and a non-smoker at BMI 30 is $22,833. The ordinary 95% range is $22,182 to $23,484. The paired resampling range is $22,045 to $23,566. The ordinary and paired ranges agree.

The same contrast is $15,643 at BMI 25 ($14,768 to $16,517) and $30,024 at BMI 35 ($29,239 to $30,809). The gap widens by about $1,461 for each additional BMI point among smokers. The non-smoker BMI slope is $23 per point, and that ordinary range includes zero (-$28 to $73).

Holding age, BMI, smoking status, and region fixed, each additional child is associated with $512 higher mean charges ($296 to $729).

These are observational contrasts. Nothing was assigned. The interval is a statement about mean charges given the sample.

Region Shift

The smoker gap does not clearly depend on region (p = 0.308). The age slope does not clearly depend on region (p = 0.279). The BMI slope among smokers does not clearly depend on region (p = 0.197).

The BMI slope among non-smokers does differ by region (p = 0.011). From the fit that allows it, the southeast non-smoker BMI slope is -$173 per point relative to the northeast (ordinary 95% range -$291 to -$55). Both slopes are small next to the smoker slope of about $1,461 per point, which is evidence against including the product in this equation.

For regional comparison only, holding age, children, BMI, and smoking status fixed, the southeast average is -$1,207 relative to the northeast (-$1,959 to -$455), about 9.1% of the average bill. The southwest contrast is -$1,228 (-$1,978 to -$477). The northwest range includes zero (-$1,327 to $170).

Unique Variation

The sample includes a unique spread or errors because this equation may be confounded by variables in the population which our sample does not represent, such as hospitals used and pre-existing conditions. Inclusion of these variables are controversial, but would improve margin of error in linear models such as this one.

  facet_wrap(~scale, scales = "free_x") +

    values = smoker_colors,
    labels = c("Non-smoker", "Smoker")
  ) +
  labs(

print(p_scales)

ggsave(
  "figures/residuals_three_scales.png",
  p_scales, width = 9, height = 3.8, dpi = 160, bg = "white"
)

On the dollar scale, smoker errors are about 1.25 times as wide as non-smoker errors The log scale flips that problem and, more importantly, provides significant evidence against a common age slope (< 0.001). A common percent-per-year is too steep for smokers, who already sit on higher bills, so their log residuals fall with age. Putting a different age slope into the log equation removes the trend and makes the spreads unequal again (smoker-to-non-smoker residual SD ratio about 0.54).

The distribution of charges get closer to a straight normal plot on the log scale. The square root only partly cuts the skew. Once the equation is fit, the leftover residuals do not follow charges. Original scale and the square root leave almost the same right-skewed residual shape. The log lowers that skew and still leaves the upper tail: a cloud of non-smokers whose charges land in the smoker range. There is no data-error reason to delete these values. The largest Cook’s distance is 0.055, against a screen of \(4/n \approx 0.003\) that flags 92 rows at this sample size. 48 rows have a studentized residual beyond 3 in absolute value. They are almost all non-smokers. Nothing in the sample helps explain these special cases.

The dollar intervals above use ordinary least-squares standard errors. Residual spread is not constant, and the upper tail is heavy, so those intervals are approximate. Using paired resampling matches the residual plot, which represents the unique variation specific to our sample. Smoker residual SD is about $5,717. Non-smoker residual SD is about $4,588.

Pricing the next customer

Explaining an average difference and pricing one new customer are different jobs. For pricing, we compare it with more flexible fits and keep the method with the smallest typical (median) dollar miss.

We use two checks to illustrate differences in bias and variance for each model. The repeated check fits on nine tenths of the customers and scores the tenth left out, then rotates, using the same ten groups every time. The held-out fifth is one 80/20 split: 1072 customers to fit, 265 to score once. When the two checks disagree, we follow the repeated check, since one split can move.

The methods, in the order they were fit:

  • The explanation equation, fit on the training customers only when it is being scored.
  • Every product of two recorded fields. This is the complicated linear model, not including polynomial transformations.
  • A search starting from the full set of products and adds or drops one term at a time, scoring by Akaike information criterion (AIC). The search is repeated inside each tenth. Otherwise the customers being scored would have helped choose the terms.
  • A penalized (shrinking) version of the same full set of products. By shrinking each variables coefficient, the optimized model is selected. The penalty can set a coefficient to exactly zero. We keep the strongest penalty that stays within one standard error of the lowest cross-validated squared error.
  • Nearest neighbors on the raw fields, including sex, after centering and scaling. Without that scaling, distance would be mostly age and BMI, and the neighborhood would ignore smoking.
  • An average of trees. Each tree may use every field at a split.
  • A random forest. Each split may look at only some of the fields. The forest below uses 500 trees and 5 fields at a split.
show_num <- function(x, digits) {
  ifelse(
    is.na(x),
    "—",
    formatC(round(x, digits), format = "f", big.mark = ",", digits = digits)
  )
}
exec_table <- data.frame(
  Model = compare$model,
  "Adjusted R2" = show_num(compare$adj_r2, 3),
  "CV ($)" = show_num(compare$cv_rmse, 0),
  "80/20 ($)" = show_num(compare$valid_rmse, 0),
  check.names = FALSE
)

Adjusted \(R^2\) is an in-sample score for the three linear fits on 1072 customers. The last two columns rank using the median of each method. AIC, BIC, and the leave-one-out PRESS statistic for the linear fits are in the appendix.

The picture below is used to illustrate a trade off between bias and variation. Using one customer: age 39, one child, female, northeast, each colored line is the quote the method would predict. Gray points are real customers within five years of that age. A straight line that sits off the cloud is bias: the method cannot follow the shape. A line that jumps from one BMI to the next is variance: the quote is chasing this sample. Linear methods can tilt, and they can tilt differently for smokers, but they stay straight. Neighbors, averaged trees, and the forest are allowed to bend.

print(p_shape)

For a non-smoker the lines sit in the lower cloud. They do not rise to the customers whose bills are far above that band. Nearest neighbors wiggle toward a few of those points and then fall back. The wiggle does not explain the band.

For a smoker the straight lines keep climbing, past $60,000 at the top of the BMI range. The cloud does not. The forest, the neighbors, and the averaged trees step up around a BMI of 30 and then level off near the cloud. The straight line is biased high once BMI is high. The flexible lines follow the step. The neighbors still jump from one BMI to the next. The forest is the calmest of the lines that are allowed to bend.

Both mean & median checks pick the random forest.

The full set of products has a repeated error of $4,842, against $4,816 for the explanation. Leaving every product in the equation does not help on either score.

What we would use

Use the random forest to price a new customer. The lowest repeated-check miss is the random forest, at $4,624. The lowest held-out miss is the random forest, at $4,366. The two checks agree. The forest is only $192 below the explanation equation on the repeated check. That gap sits inside the fold-to-fold variation of about $763. The accuracy edge is small. The reason to score with the forest is that point estimate together with the residual plot: one error bar does not fit both groups.

Keep the explanation equation for the meeting. A one-year age difference, the smoker difference at a stated BMI, and the regional level shifts are readable there. The paired ranges are what we would quote for the age amount and for the smoker gap at BMI 30. They are not readable from a forest or from a neighbor average.

We would not put the linear equation into production as the scorer. The forest does not need the constant-spread assumption that the residual plot rejects. We also would not describe the forest as an explanation. It does not say how many dollars a year of age is worth.

On the held-out fifth, 16 non-smokers have charges above $15,000. The explanation equation misses that group by about $14,036 on average. The forest misses them by about $13,554. A more flexible scorer does not explain those customers. They remain a limit of every method in this comparison.

Scope

The file supports an association in these customers. It does not support a national rate, a causal effect, or a single error bar.

The four regions are the four labels in the file. Generalizing past them is a guess. There is no household, plan, or year identifier, so we cannot check whether one customer’s bill is tied to another. Independence is an assumption, not a result.

Cause. Smoking, BMI, and region were not assigned. A smoker at BMI 30 costs about $22,833 more in this file, holding age, children, and region fixed. That is not an estimate of what the bill would do if a particular customer stopped smoking.

The forest’s margin is $9,800 for smokers and $12,486 for non-smokers, in the sense that 95% of left-out charges fell inside that distance of the quote. The explanation equation’s own errors have a standard deviation of about $5,717 for smokers and $4,588 for non-smokers, and those two spreads are not a pricing margin.

The unexplained band. High-charge non-smokers are still high-charge non-smokers after every method in this notebook. If we had more time, we would ask what the file does not contain: diagnosis, plan design, deductible, and whether the charge is one year or many. We would not add a method outside the ones compared here. We would also want a later book of customers, not another split of this one, before treating the forest’s edge of about $192 as stable.

Final recommendations: Explain with the dollar equation: age, children, a smoker gap that depends on BMI, and a regional level shift. Price with the random forest prediction model. Say the range on the two average effects with the paired resample, for a more narrow spread. A customer quits smoking or moved to the northeast from the southeast is not represented in either model.

Appendix

Squared left-out misses. Each customer’s contribution to mean squared error is the square of (bill minus quote). The histograms are the technical view of the margin in the pricing section. The horizontal axis is millions of squared dollars, so a few large misses dominate the average. That is why the meeting quote is the 95% dollar margin, not the average of the squares.

Spread of the explanation-equation misses. The ordinary range assumes one common normal spread. The residual bootstrap redraws from one pool and lines up with that assumption. The paired range does not. The paired range is the one that matches the residual plot.

set.seed(1234)
paired_sd_all <- numeric(1000)
paired_sd_no <- numeric(1000)
paired_sd_yes <- numeric(1000)
for (b in 1:1000) {
  rows <- sample.int(nrow(ins), replace = TRUE)
  fit_b <- lm(explain_formula, data = ins[rows, ])
  miss <- resid(fit_b)
  smoker_b <- ins$smoker[rows]
  paired_sd_all[b] <- sd(miss)
  paired_sd_no[b] <- sd(miss[smoker_b == "no"])
  paired_sd_yes[b] <- sd(miss[smoker_b == "yes"])
}
set.seed(1234)
resid_sd_boot <- numeric(1000)
for (b in 1:1000) {
  resid_sd_boot[b] <- sd(sample(resid_all, replace = TRUE))
}
ord_all <- sigma_ci(resid_all)
ord_no <- sigma_ci(resid_all[ins$smoker == "no"])
ord_yes <- sigma_ci(resid_all[ins$smoker == "yes"])

pair_no <- quantile(paired_sd_no, c(0.025, 0.975))
pair_yes <- quantile(paired_sd_yes, c(0.025, 0.975))

For the forest, 95% of smoker errors are within $9,800, and 95% of non-smoker errors are within $12,486. The middle 95% runs from -$4,668 to $16,014 for smokers and from -$5,051 to $16,500 for non-smokers. The explanation equation’s 95% margins are $9,489 for smokers and $13,031 for non-smokers. Stepwise Regression

The term search keeps 15 terms, against 8 in the explanation equation and 33 in the full product model. The product of BMI and smoking status is still there. Sex, which the explanation left out, is in the searched equation. Training AIC is 21,258.4, which is better than the explanation equation, because that is the score the search was asked to optimize. The repeated-check miss is $4,836. AIC rewards the equation the search built. It does not answer whether a new customer is priced more accurately. The searched equation is not the explanation equation.

Penalized Regression

The shrunk equation keeps 14 of 33 terms and has a repeated-check miss of $5,050. Shrinking the long equation does not beat the short one already chosen for explanation. The picture of that penalty is below. Farther right is a stronger penalty. The error barely changes between the penalty with the smallest squared error (25 terms) and the penalty we keep. Farther right, once only a few terms remain, the error climbs. The penalty has started to remove signal.

pen <- data.frame(
  log_penalty = log(lasso_cv_fit$lambda),
  mse = lasso_cv_fit$cvm,
  se = lasso_cv_fit$cvsd,
  nzero = lasso_cv_fit$nzero
)
p_pen <- ggplot(pen, aes(x = log_penalty, y = mse / 1e6)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = (mse - se) / 1e6, ymax = (mse + se) / 1e6),
    width = 0, color = "grey75"
  ) +
  geom_point(color = "#9B2335", size = 1.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log(lasso_cv_fit$lambda.min), linetype = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log(lasso_cv_fit$lambda.1se), linetype = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "A stronger penalty does not buy a smaller dollar miss",
    subtitle = "Left dotted line: smallest squared error. Right dotted line: the penalty we keep.",
    x = "Log penalty. Right is stronger.",
    y = "Cross-validated squared error (millions)"
  )
print(p_pen)

ggsave("figures/penalty.png", p_pen, width = 8, height = 4.4, dpi = 160, bg = "white")

kNN Details

Nearest neighbors are more flexible than a straight line and, on this file, less accurate than the explanation equation. A neighborhood of 1 has a repeated-check miss of $6,460. A neighborhood of 30 has $5,879. The size the repeated check chose is \(k = 7\), with a miss of $5,384. Copying the nearest customer is unstable. Averaging people who are not alike is stable and off. The chosen neighborhood did not pass the explanation equation. There is no coefficient list for this method. The price is an average of neighbors.

k_plot <- knn_cv$results
k_plot$choice <- ifelse(k_plot$k == k_chosen, "Chosen", "Tried")
p_knn <- ggplot(k_plot, aes(x = k, y = RMSE)) +
  geom_line(color = "#5C6B73") +
  geom_point(aes(shape = choice), size = 2.4, color = "#1F4E5F") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(Chosen = 16, Tried = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Neighbor size: too small is noisy, too large is biased",
    x = "Number of neighbors",
    y = "Repeated-check miss ($)",
    shape = NULL
  )
print(p_knn)

ggsave("figures/knn_k.png", p_knn, width = 8, height = 4, dpi = 160, bg = "white")

Averaged trees, which may use every field at a split, have a repeated-check miss of $4,867 and a held-out miss of $4,448. They beat the explanation equation on the one split and lose to it on the repeated check. That is why one split is not enough.

The forest restricts each split to 5 fields. That restriction is why its miss is not the averaged-tree miss. More flexibility is not automatically better. The gain that does show up comes from a method that can change shape, not from a longer linear equation.

The explanation equation, the full product model, the penalty, the neighbor scaling, the forest, the split, and the seed are the ones already settled.
